## Warm-up 🔥 {.smaller}

⏱️ 10 min · in the chat

1. Open your terminal and go into your `programming-basics` folder
2. Run:

```bash
git log --oneline
```

3. How many commits do you have? Write the number in the chat 🔢

::: notes
0–10 min. Quick check who managed the homework. If someone has 0 commits — pair them with someone who has 2.
:::

## Why the terminal? 💻 {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Clicking**

- Rename 300 files → 300 × click
- "Which files did I already process?"
- Impossible to repeat exactly
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Terminal**

- One line for 300 files
- The command *is* the record of what you did
- Runs on the server where your data lives 🧬
:::
::::

::: notes
10–20 min block starts here. Mention: sequencing data lives on remote servers — there is no mouse there. We will log into a real server at the end of today.
:::

## Terminal ≠ shell 🐚 {.smaller}

- **Terminal** = the window you type in
- **Shell** = the program *inside* it that understands your commands
- The most common shell: **Bash** (*Bourne Again SHell*) — macOS uses **zsh**, almost the same for us

```bash
echo $SHELL      # which shell am I using?
```

. . .

`echo` prints text · `$SHELL` is a **variable** — a name that stores a value

::: notes
Ask for the answers in the chat: /bin/bash, /bin/zsh, /usr/bin/bash (Git Bash)… Reassure: everything today works the same in all of them.
:::

## Anatomy of a command 🔬 {.smaller}

```bash
ls   -l -a   data/
#│    │       └── argument: WHAT to work on
#│    └────────── options: HOW (start with -)
#└─────────────── command: WHAT to do
```

. . .

`ls -l -a` = `ls -la` — short options can be combined

. . .

**Reading documentation:** in help pages you will see

- `<something>` → **required**, replace with a real value
- `[something]` → **optional**

```bash
man ls        # the manual (q = quit)
ls --help     # short help (works also in Git Bash)
```

::: notes
The <> / [] convention will come back in the SSH part: ssh [-p <port>] <user>@<host>.
On Git Bash `man` is often missing → use --help.
:::

## Where am I? 🗺️

The file system is a tree — you are always standing **somewhere** in it.

```bash
pwd          # print working directory — where am I?
ls           # list — what is here?
ls -l        # long: size, date
ls -a        # all: also hidden files (.git!)
```

::: notes
20–25 min. Show that `.git` is a hidden folder — that's where the whole history lives. Hidden = name starts with a dot.
:::

## Paths: two ways to say where 🧭 {.smaller}

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  H["~ (home)"] --> PB[programming-basics]
  H --> D[Downloads]
  PB --> DATA[data]
  PB --> RES[results]
  DATA --> S[sample.txt]
```

| | Example | Starts from |
|---|---|---|
| **absolute** | `/home/anna/programming-basics/data` | the root `/` |
| **relative** | `data/sample.txt` · `../Downloads` | where you are now |

`.` = here · `..` = one level up · `~` = home

::: notes
Ask: I'm in `data`. What is the relative path to `Downloads`? (../../Downloads)
:::

## Moving around 🚶

```bash
cd kse           # go into a folder
cd ..            # one level UP
cd ~             # go home
cd -             # back to where I was
```

. . .

**Tab** ⇥ completes names · **↑** repeats the last command · **Ctrl+C** stops anything

::: notes
Insist on Tab — it is the single biggest quality-of-life improvement for beginners, and it prevents typos. Ctrl+C = the emergency exit.
:::

## Exercise 1: Find your way 🧭 {.smaller}

⏱️ 10 min · your own screen · react ✅ when done

1. `pwd` — where are you now? Is this an absolute or relative path?
2. Go home: `cd ~`
3. `ls` — what folders do you see?
4. Go into your `programming-basics` folder
5. `ls -a` — can you find the `.git` folder?
6. Go one level up, then back — using **Tab** at least once

💡 **Bonus:** what does `ls -lh` show that `ls -l` doesn't? Find out with `ls --help`.

::: notes
25–35 min. Paste steps in the chat. Watch reactions; anyone with ✋ shares their screen.
:::

## Making and moving things 🧰

```bash
mkdir data              # make a folder
mkdir -p a/b/c          # make nested folders at once
touch notes.txt         # make an empty file
cp notes.txt backup.txt # copy
mv notes.txt data/      # move (also = rename!)
rm backup.txt           # delete a file
rm -r old_folder        # delete a folder with everything inside
```

. . .

::: {.callout-warning}
`rm` does **not** use a trash bin. Deleted is deleted. 💀
:::

::: notes
35–45 min. Tell a short real story about deleting something important. Then: this is exactly why we use Git.
:::

## Wildcards: many files at once 🃏 {.smaller}

| Pattern | Matches | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `*` | anything (also nothing) | `ls *.txt` |
| `?` | exactly one character | `ls sample?.txt` |
| `[12]` | one of these characters | `ls sample[12].txt` |

. . .

**Brace expansion** — the shell writes the list for you:

```bash
mkdir -p project/{data,scripts,results}   # 3 folders, 1 line
touch sample{1..5}.txt                    # sample1.txt … sample5.txt
```

. . .

⚠️ `rm *` — think twice. Check first with `ls *` 👀

::: notes
Key idea: the SHELL expands the pattern before the command even sees it. `ls *.txt` — ls receives a list of names.
Safe habit: run the pattern with `ls` first, then replace `ls` with `rm`.
:::

## Looking inside files 👀

```bash
cat notes.txt             # print the whole file
head sequences.fasta      # first 10 lines
head -n 3 sequences.fasta # first 3 lines
tail sequences.fasta      # last 10 lines
less sequences.fasta      # scroll (q = quit!)
wc -l sequences.fasta     # count lines
```

. . .

In `less`: **space** = next page, **/word** = search, **q** = quit 🙂

::: notes
`cat` is fine for small files; on a 3 GB FASTA it will flood your screen → Ctrl+C. Everyone gets stuck in `less` at least once. Say "q" twice.
:::

## Exercise 2: Build a project 🏗️ {.smaller}

⏱️ 20 min · breakout rooms · one shares the screen, switch after 10 min

Inside `programming-basics`:

1. Create folders `data`, `scripts`, `results` — **in one command**
2. In `data`, create `sample.txt` with 3 lines of text
   (`nano sample.txt`, then **Ctrl+O**, **Enter**, **Ctrl+X**)
3. Check with `head` and `wc -l` that it has 3 lines
4. Copy it to `results/sample_copy.txt`, then rename it to `results/backup.txt`
5. Create `test1.txt` … `test5.txt` in `results` with one command, then delete them all with **one** `rm`
6. `git add` → `git commit` → `git push`

💡 **Bonus:** what happens in Git with the **empty** `scripts` folder? Why?

::: notes
45–65 min. Steps 1 and 5 practise brace expansion + wildcards.
The bonus is a great discussion: Git tracks files, not folders — empty folders never appear on GitHub (convention: put an empty `.gitkeep` inside).
Plan B for nano trouble: create the file in VS Code / any editor.
:::

## Servers: computers without a screen 🖥️ {.smaller}

- Genome data = hundreds of GB → it lives on a **server** (university cluster, cloud)
- You don't sit in front of it — you **log in remotely** and get a terminal *there*
- The tool: **SSH** (*Secure Shell*) — an encrypted connection

```bash
ssh [-p <port>] <user>@<host>
```

. . .

```bash
ssh -p 2220 bandit0@bandit.labs.overthewire.org
```

- First time: *"Are you sure you want to continue connecting?"* → type `yes`
- Typing the password shows **nothing** — no dots, no stars. That's normal 🙈
- `exit` → back to your own computer

::: notes
65–68 min. Works in macOS/Linux Terminal, Git Bash and Windows PowerShell (OpenSSH is built into Windows 10/11).
Point out the prompt change: after login it shows bandit0@bandit — a different computer!
:::

## Exercise 3: Your first server 🔐 {.smaller}

⏱️ 10 min · together, everyone on their own screen

**OverTheWire Bandit** — a real server, built as a game for learning the terminal

1. Log in: `ssh -p 2220 bandit0@bandit.labs.overthewire.org` (password: `bandit0`)
2. `whoami` · `pwd` · `hostname` — where are you now?
3. `ls` — there is a file. Read it with `cat`
4. That's the password for the next level (`bandit1`) 🎉
5. `exit`

. . .

🚫 **Don't post passwords in the chat** — that spoils the game for others

::: notes
68–78 min. Do it live first, then everyone repeats. If the university network blocks port 2220, mobile hotspot usually works; otherwise it becomes homework.
Levels 1–4 use exactly today's commands: `cat ./-` (strange filename), quotes for spaces, `ls -a` (hidden file), `file ./*`.
:::

## What we learned ✅ {.smaller}

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `pwd` `ls` `cd` | Where am I, what's here, move |
| `mkdir` `touch` | Make folders and files |
| `cp` `mv` `rm` | Copy, move/rename, delete |
| `cat` `head` `tail` `less` `wc` | Look inside, count |
| `*` `?` `{a,b}` | Many files at once |
| `ssh user@host` | Log into another computer |
